strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem: reasoning models are decode-dominated, so calibrating pruning on prompt-only data creates a distribution mismatch that standard LLM pruning pipelines ignore.
Simple, practical, drop-in method (RAC) that integrates directly into existing pruning algorithms like SparseGPT without retraining or distillation.
Reasonably comprehensive experiments across four model scales (1.5B-32B), multiple sparsity levels (20-50%), and two task domains (math via MATH500, code via LiveCodeBench/CodeForces).
Useful mechanistic analysis (Figure 2, tokenwise reconstruction error heatmap) showing RAC specifically reduces error during the decode phase on held-out problems, supporting the core hypothesis.

Thoughtful ablations: on-policy vs off-policy CoT traces, combination with semi-structured 2:4 sparsity and FP8 quantization, and the effect of maximum decode budget on runtime overhead, which nicely explains and partially resolves the counterintuitive 'pruning makes inference slower' phenomenon.
The runtime analysis is a distinguishing and practically relevant contribution beyond pure accuracy numbers, which many pruning papers ignore.
weaknesses: Only one base pruning algorithm (SparseGPT) is evaluated with RAC; despite claiming general applicability to WANDA/GPTQ-style methods, no experiments confirm this beyond a brief mention.

All experiments use a single model family (Qwen distilled from DeepSeek-R1); generality to other reasoning model architectures/training recipes (e.g., different distillation processes or natively RL-trained reasoning models) is untested.

Method novelty is somewhat incremental: it is essentially 'calibrate on self-generated rollouts instead of prompts only,' which is a reasonably natural extension of existing calibration-data literature (e.g., Bandari et al. 2024) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The added cost of generating full on-policy CoT rollouts (up to 8192 tokens) for calibration is only briefly acknowledged as a limitation without quantitative overhead reporting (e.g., wall-clock or GPU-hours compared to prompt-only calibration).

Some presentation/data issues: a missing dense baseline entry in Table 1 (32B, 50%, C4), a formatting typo in Table 3, and results discussion sometimes reads as a narrative restatement of table numbers rather than deeper analysis.

No comparison against alternative reasoning-aware compression baselines (e.g., PPC-GPT distillation-based approach mentioned in related work) to contextualize the magnitude of RAC's improvement relative to other reasoning-specific compression strategies.

The structured/quantization ablation (Table 4) is limited to a single model size (14B) and lacks error bars or repeated trials for throughput measurements, making claims about throughput gains less rigorously supported.

strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates a real, underexplored problem: standard LLM pruning calibration is prompt-centric, but reasoning models are decode-dominated, causing disproportionate accuracy loss and even inference slowdowns after pruning.

The proposed fix (RAC) is simple, well-motivated theoretically (matching calibration activation distribution to the on-policy decode-time distribution), and integrates as a drop-in replacement in existing one-shot pruning pipelines (e.g., SparseGPT) without retraining or distillation.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across model scales (1.5B to 32B Qwen/DeepSeek-R1-Distill models), two task domains (math via MATH500, code via LiveCodeBench/CodeGen), and several sparsity levels, showing consistent and sometimes large gains from RAC over C4 and prompt-only calibration, especially at high sparsity.

The tokenwise reconstruction-error analysis on held-out problems (Figure 2) provides a nice diagnostic that directly supports the paper's causal story—that RAC's advantage stems from better matching decode-time activations, not merely overlap with calibration data.

Useful ablations, including on-policy vs. off-policy CoT calibration, combination with structured 2:4 sparsity and FP8 quantization, and analysis of how bounding max decode length changes the runtime/accuracy tradeoff, which help contextualize when RAC's benefits matter most.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core idea is essentially changing the calibration corpus to include self-generated CoT rollouts, which is a natural, fairly predictable extension once the decode-dominated framing is stated (and related work such as Bandari et al. already shows calibration data choice matters greatly); no fundamentally new pruning objective or algorithm is proposed.

Evaluation is narrow in terms of pruning methods: only SparseGPT is evaluated in the main results, despite the paper mentioning WANDA and ALPS as being compatible; no results confirm RAC generalizes beyond one specific pruning algorithm.

Missing comparisons to other reasoning-aware or CoT-preserving compression baselines beyond the paper's own prompt-only/C4 ablations (e.g., no comparison with teacher-forced ground-truth CoT calibration instead of self-generated on-policy rollouts, which would isolate whether the gain comes from on-policy generation specifically or simply from including any long CoT-like text).

The calibration cost of on-policy rollout generation (which requires running full generation for every calibration prompt, potentially thousands of tokens) is acknowledged as a limitation but never quantified in wall-clock or compute terms, making it hard to assess the real practicality tradeoff versus prompt-only calibration.

Some result tables have gaps or inconsistencies (e.g., missing C4 result at 32B/50% sparsity without explanation, missing "Entire Model" column for Prompt+FP8 in Table 4), and gains at lower sparsity (20-30%) are often within or close to overlapping standard errors, making the practical significance of RAC less clear in the low-compression regime.

The reported reduction in runtime overhead is somewhat indirect and partially confounded: Table 5 shows that capping max decode length largely eliminates the runtime penalty for both dense and pruned models, suggesting much of the "RAC solves runtime" narrative in the abstract/intro is really about output-length capping rather than an intrinsic property of RAC.

Code generation accuracy is reported with a relatively lenient acc@1:16 metric (correct answer anywhere in top 16 predictions), which likely overstates robustness relative to a stricter pass@1 metric more standard in the literature, and no pass@1 results are given for code.

strengths: Identifies a clear and practically important failure mode: standard prompt-only calibration for pruning reasoning LLMs causes severe accuracy loss and can paradoxically increase inference latency due to longer, degenerate CoT traces at high sparsity.

The proposed fix (RAC) is simple, well-motivated theoretically (formalizes the mismatch between calibration activation distribution and true decode-time activation distribution), and integrates as a drop-in replacement into existing one-shot pruning pipelines (SparseGPT, WANDA, ALPS) without retraining.

Very extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple model families and sizes (DeepSeek-R1-distill Qwen 1.5B-32B, DeepSeek-R1-distill Llama 8B/70B, Qwen3 1.7B-14B), multiple sparsity levels, multiple benchmarks (MATH500, AIME-25, LiveCodeBench), and multiple pruning algorithms, showing generally consistent gains from RAC especially at higher sparsity.

Useful ablations: on-policy vs off-policy CoT traces, structured 2:4 pruning combined with FP8 quantization, effect of decode-length budget on runtime, and a token-wise reconstruction-error analysis on held-out problems that mechanistically supports the claimed benefit of RAC during the decode phase.

Clear and reasonably rigorous positioning against related work (concurrent benchmarking study, self-calibration, calibration-dataset studies), correctly distinguishing RAC's use of task-conditioned on-policy CoT activations from prior approaches.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is incremental relative to existing self-calibration approaches (Williams et al., 2025) and prompt-only calibration baselines already tested in this paper; the contribution is largely combining/extending known ideas (on-policy generation, CoT-aware calibration) rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The paper does not quantify the additional computational cost of collecting on-policy CoT activations (which requires full autoregressive rollouts up to 8192 tokens per calibration prompt) relative to standard single-pass prompt calibration; this is asserted to be 'modest' without supporting numbers, which is important since decode is far more expensive than prefill.

Benchmarks used for fine-grained comparisons (MATH500 with 500 problems, AIME-25 with only 30 problems) yield large standard errors, and many reported differences between RAC and baselines—particularly at lower sparsity levels (20-30%)—fall within overlapping confidence intervals, raising questions about the statistical robustness of some claimed improvements.

Results appear to be based on a single pruning/calibration run per configuration (no repeated calibration seeds or multiple pruning masks reported), limiting the ability to assess variance introduced by the pruning process itself as opposed to evaluation noise.

Some presented results are not fully explained or are internally inconsistent (e.g., Table 6 structured-pruning+quantization results show accuracy dropping noticeably for 'Entire Model' RAC+FP8 despite higher throughput, and several missing values/baselines are not discussed).

No comparison to alternative or complementary efficiency approaches for reasoning models (e.g., distillation-based shortening of CoT, speculative decoding, or learned length control) that could contextualize how competitive one-shot pruning with RAC is against other deployment-cost-reduction strategies.

Reproducibility details are somewhat sparse (e.g., exact number of calibration prompts/CoT samples per model, compute budget for RAC's activation collection phase, and hyperparameters for baselines like ALPS/WANDA) and code is only promised, not verifiable at review time.
